title: Price Output Determination under Different Market Forms
outcomes: Explain short-run and long-run equilibrium of a firm and an industry under perfect competition, including supernormal profit, normal profit, losses and the shut-down point.
Explain how monopolies arise, derive the monopolist's AR and MR, and determine its price, output and profit; analyse price discrimination and the economic effects of monopoly.
Explain short-run and long-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition, including excess capacity, and compare the three market forms.
Describe the types and characteristics of oligopoly, and the main models — collusion and cartels, price leadership and the kinked demand curve — and other market forms.

meta.exam_tip: This is the heaviest unit of the chapter: expect 5–8 MCQs. Know the comparison table cold, the equilibrium conditions (MR = MC, MC rising), long-run results (normal profit, excess capacity), conditions and degrees of price discrimination, and the kinked demand curve logic.

concepts.title: Perfect competition — features
body: Features: (i) a very large number of buyers and sellers, each too small to affect price; (ii) a homogeneous product — the output of every firm is a perfect substitute for every other, so one price rules; (iii) free entry and exit — no legal, cost or market barriers. A market with only these three features is called pure competition (the essence is absence of any monopoly element).

Perfect competition adds: (iv) perfect knowledge of prices, quantities and quality among buyers and sellers; (v) negligible transaction costs; (vi) every firm (and every buyer) is a price taker — if a seller asks more than the ruling price, he loses his customers. Textbooks also assume perfect mobility of factors, no government interference and no collusion.
Truly perfect markets are rare (many call them a myth), but farm produce in a large mandi, shares and foreign exchange on exchanges, and gold or silver come close.
concepts.analogy: Hundreds of potato sellers in one mandi, all with the same potatoes and all asking ₹20 a kg — anyone asking ₹22 sells nothing; nobody needs to ask ₹18.
concepts.work: In commodity businesses (steel billets, cotton, basic chemicals) margins depend almost entirely on cost control because the firm cannot set its price — a key point in credit appraisal.

concepts.title: Equilibrium of the industry and of the firm
body: Industry equilibrium: total quantity supplied by all firms equals total quantity demanded; the price at that point is the market price, which every firm must accept.

Because the firm can sell any quantity at that price, its demand (AR) curve is a horizontal line at the market price — perfectly elastic. Every extra unit adds exactly the price to revenue, so P = AR = MR. The firm decides only how much to produce, not the price.

Firm equilibrium (maximum profit) needs two conditions: (i) MR = MC, which for a competitive firm means P = MC; and (ii) MC must cut MR from below (MC rising). Where MC cuts MR while falling, profit is at a minimum, not a maximum.

Short-run supply curve: at each price the firm produces where P = MC, so its MC curve traces how much it supplies at each price — but only the part of the MC curve above minimum AVC. Below minimum AVC it supplies nothing.
concepts.analogy: The price line is a flat shelf at the market price; the firm keeps adding units until the cost of the next unit climbs above that shelf.
concepts.work: Capacity-expansion proposals in commodity firms are tested by asking: at the forecast market price, where does our marginal cost cross it? That gives the realistic output, not the nameplate capacity.

concepts.title: Short run: supernormal profit, normal profit or loss
body: Normal profit is the minimum return an entrepreneur must earn to stay in the business — the opportunity cost of his own capital and effort. Economists include it in cost (as an implicit cost), so when AR = ATC the firm earns normal profit, i.e. zero economic profit.
Supernormal (economic) profit: AR > ATC at the equilibrium output; profit per unit = AR − ATC and total profit = (AR − ATC) × Q.

Loss: AR < ATC at the equilibrium output. The firm still produces (it is minimising loss) as long as price covers AVC, because it recovers some fixed cost. If price is below minimum AVC, it shuts down temporarily and loses only its fixed cost.
So in the short run a competitive firm in equilibrium may earn supernormal profit, normal profit or a loss — it depends on where the market price stands relative to its ATC and AVC.
concepts.analogy: A chartered bus: if fares cover diesel and the driver (variable cost), it runs even when the loan instalment (fixed cost) is not fully covered; if fares do not cover diesel, it stays in the depot.
concepts.work: CAs often explain to clients the gap between accounting profit and economic profit: a business showing a "profit" may still not cover the return the owner could earn on his capital elsewhere.

concepts.title: Long run: firm and industry under perfect competition
body: In the long run firms can change their plant size and firms can enter or leave. Supernormal profits attract new firms; industry supply rises, price falls (and costs may rise as factor prices go up) until the profit disappears. Losses drive firms out; supply falls and price rises until the remaining firms earn normal profit.

Long-run equilibrium of the firm: price equals the minimum of the long-run average cost curve, where the LAC is tangent to the horizontal demand line: P = LMC = LAC. At that point the plant is worked at its optimal capacity, so SMC = LMC = SAC = LAC = P = MR.

Long-run equilibrium of the industry needs three things: every firm maximises profit; every firm earns only normal profit, so nobody wants to enter or leave; and industry quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.

Results (optimal allocation of resources): output produced at the lowest possible cost (optimum firms); consumers pay a price equal to marginal cost (P = MC); plants used to full capacity (MC = AC, no waste); only normal profit (AR = AC); and an optimum number of firms. In short: LAR = LMR = P = LMC = LAC.
concepts.analogy: A food street where one new dish earns big profits: within months ten stalls copy it, the price drifts down, and soon each stall earns just enough to stay open.
concepts.work: When valuing a firm in a highly competitive industry, analysts assume excess returns will fade towards the cost of capital over time — the long-run "normal profit" result in practice.

concepts.title: Monopoly — features and how it arises
body: Monopoly means a single seller of a product that has no close substitute. Features: (1) one firm, so firm and industry are the same; (2) strong barriers to entry — economic, legal, institutional or artificial; (3) no close substitutes, so cross elasticity with other goods is zero or very small and its demand curve falls steeply; (4) market power — the ability to set price above marginal cost. The monopolist is a price maker.

Sources of monopoly (barriers): control of a scarce input, resource or technology; a unique product that is hard or costly to copy; exclusive rights granted by government; patents and copyrights; business combinations and cartels; huge start-up costs or costly know-how; natural monopoly (economies of scale so large that one firm can supply the whole market at a lower cost than two or more, as in power distribution, piped gas or telephone lines); long-standing goodwill; strict licensing and regulation; and predatory tactics such as limit pricing.
Pure monopoly is rare because monopolies are usually regulated or prohibited. In India, rail transport by Indian Railways and nuclear power generation by the government are examples.
concepts.analogy: The only bridge across a river: everyone who wants to cross pays the toll you set — but set it too high and fewer people cross.
concepts.work: Competition-law work (merger filings, abuse-of-dominance analysis) starts with these questions: how big are the entry barriers and how close are the substitutes?

concepts.title: Monopoly revenue curves and equilibrium
body: The monopolist's demand curve is the market demand curve, and since it charges one price for all units, AR = price, so the demand curve is its AR curve. To sell more it must lower the price on all units, so MR < AR.

For a straight-line demand curve: both AR and MR slope downwards; MR has twice the slope of AR and lies halfway between the price axis and the AR curve (if P = a − bQ, then MR = a − 2bQ); AR is never zero at a positive price but MR can be zero or negative.

Equilibrium (short run): output where MR = MC with MC cutting MR from below; the price is then read off the demand (AR) curve above that output. Profit per unit = AR − ATC. A monopolist does not always earn profit: if demand is weak and ATC > AR it makes a loss; it continues in the short run only if AVC is covered.

Long run: the monopolist adjusts plant size. It will not stay if it makes losses, and because entry is blocked it can keep supernormal profit. It need not produce at the minimum point of LAC — it may operate at a sub-optimal scale.

Because MC > 0, MR = MC requires MR > 0, so a monopolist always produces on the elastic part of the demand curve (e > 1). Monopoly may be simple (one price to all buyers) or discriminating (different prices to different buyers).
concepts.analogy: MR is a shadow that falls twice as fast as the AR line it follows.
concepts.work: Regulators setting tariffs for utilities compare the price a monopolist would charge (MR = MC) with cost-based prices; CAs prepare the cost-of-service data used in these tariff petitions.

concepts.title: Price discrimination
body: Price discrimination means selling the same product to different buyers at different prices for reasons not linked to differences in cost — e.g. a doctor charging a rich patient more, cheaper electricity for rural homes than for factories, student subscriptions, off-peak call rates, dumping abroad at lower prices.

Conditions: (I) the seller must have some monopoly (price-setting) power — necessary but not sufficient; (II) the market must be divisible into sub-markets; (III) price elasticity must differ between sub-markets; (IV) no arbitrage — buyers in the cheap market cannot resell in the dear market. It cannot persist under perfect competition.

Degrees (Pigou): first degree — each buyer is charged the maximum he is willing to pay, taking away the entire consumer surplus (negotiated fees, auctions, bid-and-offer); second degree — price differs with the quantity bought (cheaper family packs, slab tariffs for water or electricity), taking part of the consumer surplus; third degree — the market is split by location, age, use or segment (domestic vs commercial power, senior-citizen fares, dumping).

Equilibrium: MR in each market = AR(e − 1)/e. At a single price, MR is higher in the more elastic market, so the seller shifts output there until MRs are equal. Total output is fixed where the aggregate MR (horizontal sum of the sub-market MRs) = MC; output is split so that MRA = MRB = MC; the price is higher in the less elastic market.

Objectives: maximum profit, disposing of surplus stock, economies of scale, capturing foreign markets, and equity through pricing. Effects: lower consumer surplus and welfare loss since price exceeds MC; but it can keep some firms or essential services (e.g. railways) viable, spread peak-load demand, and let poorer buyers purchase at lower prices.
concepts.analogy: One flight, one seat type, many fares: the business traveller who must fly tomorrow (inelastic) pays far more than the student who booked months ahead (elastic).
concepts.work: Transfer-pricing, dynamic pricing and customer-segment profitability analyses in industry all rest on these conditions — and auditors check that discounts by segment comply with competition and consumer law.

concepts.title: Economic effects of monopoly
body: Criticisms: loss of productive and allocative efficiency; higher prices and lower output than under competition; unjustified long-run economic profit; price above MC, so consumer surplus is transferred to the monopolist; restricted consumer choice (sovereignty); costly efforts to keep rivals out raise average cost; political influence to win favourable laws; weak incentive to innovate; power to pay suppliers less; and X-inefficiency — managerial slack where competition is absent.
Because of these effects, governments try to prevent monopolies from forming and regulate those that exist.
concepts.analogy: A monopolist is like the only canteen in a remote campus: prices high, menu short, and little reason to improve the food.
concepts.work: Due-diligence reports flag a target's dominance not only as a strength but also as a regulatory risk (possible penalties or price controls).

concepts.title: Monopolistic competition
body: A blend of monopoly and perfect competition, very common in practice (soaps, clothing, restaurants, salons, retail shops in cities). Features: (i) a large number of independent sellers, each with a small market share; (ii) product differentiation — real or imagined, through brand, design, packaging, features, service — which creates brand loyalty and some monopoly power; (iii) relatively free entry and exit; (iv) non-price competition — heavy advertising, product development, better distribution and after-sales service, because price wars are risky; selling costs are vital.
Each firm is a price maker for its own brand and faces a downward-sloping but fairly elastic demand curve — the less its product is differentiated, the more elastic the curve.
Short run: MR = MC (MC cutting MR from below); the firm may earn supernormal profit or make a loss.

Long run: supernormal profits attract new brands, each firm's demand shrinks and becomes tangent to its average cost curve (AR = AC), so only normal profit is earned; persistent losses make firms leave until the rest earn normal profit. The tangency lies on the falling part of the AC curve, so each firm produces less than the output at minimum AC — it has excess capacity. Expanding output to lower AC is irrational because price would have to fall more than cost.

blocks.title: Three market forms compared

concepts.analogy: A street of cafés: each serves "its own" coffee and can charge a little more, but if one charges too much, customers walk next door.
concepts.work: Marketing-spend budgets that a CA reviews in consumer businesses are the non-price competition of this market form — tested for return like any other investment.

concepts.title: Oligopoly — types and features
body: Oligopoly is "competition among the few": a few large sellers (roughly two to ten) of homogeneous or differentiated products, where each firm's policy depends partly on what it expects its close rivals to do (Stigler). Examples: cold drinks, automobiles, airlines, petroleum refining, mobile telephony.

Types: pure (homogeneous product, e.g. steel, aluminium) vs differentiated (e.g. talcum powder); open (entry possible) vs closed (entry restricted); collusive (firms agree on price/output) vs competitive; partial (one dominant firm acts as price leader) vs full (no price leader); syndicated (sales through a central syndicate) vs organised (a central association fixes prices, output and quotas).

Characteristics: a few large firms with a big market share and strong entry barriers; strategic interdependence — any move by one firm provokes reactions; great importance of advertising and selling costs, with firms avoiding price cuts that could trigger a price war; and group behaviour — there is no single accepted theory of how the group will act.
Game theory (Von Neumann and Morgenstern, 1944) is used to analyse such strategic choices under uncertainty.
concepts.analogy: Three petrol pumps at one crossing: none dares to change its price without first guessing what the other two will do.
concepts.work: In industries like telecom or aviation, analysts read every price move as part of a strategic game — and CAs in those firms model competitor reactions in their pricing papers.

concepts.title: Oligopoly — price and output models
body: Because rivals react, an oligopolist has no single definite demand curve, so price and output cannot be found without assumptions about behaviour. Three broad approaches: (i) firms ignore interdependence — demand becomes definite and MR = MC gives the output; (ii) firms predict rivals' reactions — Cournot (output is the decision variable, no collusion), Stackelberg (a leader fixes output first, followers adjust), Bertrand (price is the decision variable); (iii) firms collude and act like one monopoly to maximise joint profit, sharing output or profit — a cartel (generally illegal; OPEC is the classic example). A cartel earns monopoly-like profit, especially when demand is inelastic, if members stick to the agreement.

Price leadership: by a dominant firm (it sets the price that maximises its profit after allowing for the output of the small fringe firms — "live and let live"); by a low-cost firm (it sets a price that still leaves some profit for followers); and barometric (an old, experienced or respected firm reads market conditions and announces changes that others accept).

Kinked demand curve (Paul Sweezy): explains why oligopoly prices are sticky. Each firm believes rivals will match a price cut but will not follow a price rise. So above the ruling price its demand is highly elastic (a rise loses many customers to rivals) and below it demand is inelastic (a cut gains few customers because rivals cut too). The demand curve has a kink at the prevailing price and each firm sticks to that price even when costs or demand change somewhat.

Other market forms: duopoly — only two sellers (a special case of oligopoly); monopsony — a single buyer, mostly of a factor; oligopsony — a few large buyers; bilateral monopoly — one buyer facing one seller.
concepts.analogy: Kinked demand: raise your price and the crowd walks to your rivals; cut it and your rivals cut too — so you leave the price board alone.
concepts.work: Competition authorities investigate parallel price moves for cartels; CAs supporting such inquiries analyse cost and price data to tell genuine price leadership from collusion.

illustrations.title: A price-taking kiosk: output, profit and shut-down price
illustrations.q: Chai Point Kiosk is a price taker. Its total cost at outputs 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 cups an hour is ₹150, 270, 360, 470, 620, 850 and 1,140. Complete TFC, TVC, AVC, AFC and MC. (a) At a price of ₹15 a cup, how many cups should it sell and what is its profit or loss? (b) At ₹23? (c) Below what price should it shut down?

head: Output (Q)
TC (₹)
TFC (₹)
TVC (₹)
AVC (₹)
AFC (₹)
MC per unit (₹)
solution.title: Costs of Chai Point Kiosk (price taker)
(a) Price ₹15
solution.text: P = MR = ₹15 = MC at 40 cups (MC rising). TR = 600, TC = 620, so a loss of ₹20 (ATC = ₹15.5 > price). It still produces because TR exceeds TVC by ₹130, which covers part of the fixed cost of ₹150.

solution.title: (c)
solution.text: Minimum AVC is ₹10.5 (at 20 cups) — the shut-down price. Below it the kiosk should stop serving for the time being.

illustrations.title: Normal profit is a cost
illustrations.q: Meher invests ₹1,00,000 of her own money in a candle unit. Explicit costs of making 2,000 boxes a month are ₹40,000. She could earn 10% a month on her money elsewhere. Find ATC (economic) and state the type of profit at prices of ₹25, ₹28 and ₹23 a box.

items: ₹28 > ATC → supernormal profit of ₹3 a box = ₹6,000 a month (accounting profit would show ₹16,000, because it ignores the implicit cost).

illustrations.title: Monopoly equilibrium vs the competitive outcome
illustrations.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − 2Q and has constant MC = AC = ₹20. Find its output, price and profit, and compare with the output and price if the industry were perfectly competitive (P = MC).

solution.text: The monopolist produces half the competitive output at three times the price. Elasticity at the monopoly point = AR ÷ (AR − MR) = 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 > 1 — the monopolist operates on the elastic part of demand.

checks.label: elasticity at monopoly equilibrium = AR/(AR - MR)

illustrations.title: Third-degree price discrimination
illustrations.q: (a) A firm charges a single price of ₹48 in two markets where the elasticities are 1.6 (market A) and 4 (market B). Find MR in each market and explain what the firm should do. (b) Later the firm estimates PA = 50 − 2QA and PB = 30 − QB, with constant MC = ₹10. Find the profit-maximising quantities and prices in each market.

solution.title: (a)
solution.text: MRA = 48 × 0.6/1.6 = ₹18; MRB = 48 × 3/4 = ₹36. Moving one unit from A to B loses ₹18 but gains ₹36 — a net gain of ₹18. The firm should shift sales to B (price in A rises, in B falls) until MRA = MRB.

solution.title: (b)
solution.text: MRA = 50 − 4QA = 10 → QA = 10, PA = ₹30. MRB = 30 − 2QB = 10 → QB = 10, PB = ₹20. Total output 20 units; MRA = MRB = MC = ₹10; total revenue ₹500.
Elasticity at equilibrium: A = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5; B = 20 ÷ 10 = 2. The higher price is charged in the less elastic market (A).

checks.label: MR in market A at single price
MR in market B at single price
gain from shifting one unit A to B

jobs.title: Pricing a new route: segment the market
jobs.role: CA in industry — revenue management at a regional airline
jobs.situation: The airline launches a new route. Business travellers book late and rarely change plans; leisure travellers book early and compare fares.
steps: Check the conditions for price discrimination: pricing power on the route, separable segments (booking date, flexibility), different elasticities, and no resale (tickets are named).
Set higher fares for late, flexible tickets (inelastic segment) and lower advance fares (elastic segment).
Allocate seats so that the marginal revenue from the last seat in each fare bucket is roughly equal.
Review for consumer-law and disclosure compliance.
jobs.takeaway: Third-degree price discrimination raises revenue when segments differ in elasticity and resale is impossible.
jobs.think: Why would the scheme fail if tickets could be freely transferred?
jobs.answer: Buyers would purchase cheap advance fares and resell them to business travellers — arbitrage would destroy the price difference.

jobs.title: Advising a café owner on the long run
jobs.role: CA in practice advising a small business
jobs.situation: A client's specialty café earned high profits last year. Five similar cafés have opened nearby and footfall is falling.
steps: Explain monopolistic competition: free entry erodes supernormal profit until only normal profit remains.
Recommend strengthening differentiation (menu, ambience, loyalty programme) rather than a price war.
Budget selling costs carefully and track their return.
Plan for capacity: in the long run the café may run below full capacity — keep fixed commitments flexible.
jobs.takeaway: In monopolistic competition, profits are temporary unless differentiation is continually renewed.

jobs.title: Spotting a possible cartel in tender data
jobs.role: Forensic accountant assisting a public-sector buyer
jobs.situation: Bids from four suppliers for the same item move up together each year, and the lowest bidder rotates.
steps: Tabulate bid prices against input-cost indices to see if increases exceed cost changes.
Look for bid rotation, identical figures and unusually narrow spreads.
Distinguish lawful price leadership (followers react to a public price) from collusion (agreed prices or quotas).
Report the pattern to management for referral to the competition authority if warranted.
jobs.takeaway: Collusive oligopoly leaves fingerprints in pricing data — economics tells you what to look for.

mcqs.q: Which feature, together with many sellers and a homogeneous product, defines "pure" competition?
mcqs.explain: Pure competition needs three conditions: a large number of buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, and free entry and exit. Perfect competition adds further conditions such as perfect knowledge and perfect mobility of factors. "Perfect knowledge" is the trap — it is what turns pure competition into perfect competition, not part of the pure-competition core. In practice: agricultural mandis come close to pure competition, though buyers rarely have perfect information.

mcqs.q: A firm under perfect competition is a:
mcqs.explain: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: its output is too small a share of the market to affect price, so it accepts the price set by industry demand and supply. "Price leader" is the trap — price leadership belongs to oligopoly, where one large firm sets prices that others follow. In practice: an individual cotton farmer cannot raise his price above the going rate at the mandi without losing every buyer.

mcqs.q: Under perfect competition, the demand curve facing an individual firm is:
mcqs.explain: Since a competitive firm can sell any quantity at the ruling market price but nothing above it, its demand curve is a horizontal line at that price — perfectly elastic. "Downward sloping" is the trap; that is the industry's market demand curve, or the demand facing a firm with some pricing power. In practice: a small rice mill can sell all it produces at the market rate, but nothing at even ₹1 more per quintal.

mcqs.q: For a perfectly competitive firm:
mcqs.explain: Every unit sells at the same market price, so average revenue equals price and each extra unit adds exactly that price to total revenue: P = AR = MR. "AR > MR" is the trap — that holds only when a firm must cut price to sell more, as under monopoly or monopolistic competition. In practice: a farmer selling 10 or 11 quintals at the MSP gets the same extra amount for the 11th quintal.

mcqs.q: The second condition for a firm's equilibrium is that:
options: MC must cut MR from below
MC must cut MR from above
mcqs.explain: MR = MC is necessary for equilibrium, but at that output MC must also cut MR from below (MC rising); otherwise producing more would add more to revenue than to cost. "MC must cut MR from above" is the trap — where falling MC meets MR, profit is at a minimum, not a maximum. In practice: a factory expands output while the extra cost per unit is below the price, and stops once it rises above.

mcqs.q: The short-run supply curve of a competitive firm is:
options: The part of its MC curve above minimum AVC
mcqs.explain: A competitive firm produces where P = MC, so its MC curve shows how much it supplies at each price — but only above minimum AVC; below that price it shuts down and supplies nothing. "Its entire MC curve" is the trap — the part below minimum AVC is irrelevant, as the firm would not produce there. In practice: seasonal brick kilns stop firing when prices fall below their running costs.

mcqs.q: When AR = ATC at the equilibrium output, a firm earns:
mcqs.explain: If AR = ATC at equilibrium, total revenue just covers total cost, including normal profit (which economists count as a cost). So economic profit is zero and the firm earns normal profit. "A loss" is the trap — a loss arises only when AR is below ATC. In practice: many small traders earn just enough to match what they could get in a job — normal profit with no surplus.

mcqs.q: A competitive firm making a loss in the short run will continue production if:
options: Price is at least equal to AVC
mcqs.explain: In the short run, fixed cost is lost even if the firm shuts down. If price at least covers AVC, producing covers variable cost and perhaps some fixed cost, so the loss is no bigger than shutting down. "Price is below AVC" is the trap — then each unit adds to the loss, and shutting down is better. In practice: hotels in the off-season stay open as long as room rates cover staff, power and supplies.

mcqs.q: A competitive firm produces 400 units where P = MC = ₹30. Its ATC at 400 units is ₹26. Its supernormal profit is:
mcqs.explain: Supernormal profit = (AR − ATC) × Q = (30 − 26) × 400 = 4 × 400 = ₹1,600. ₹12,000 is the trap — it is total revenue (30 × 400); ₹10,400 is total cost (26 × 400). In practice: a firm earning ₹4 above full cost per unit, including a normal return, attracts new competitors, which is why such profits tend to vanish in the long run.

mcqs.q: In long-run equilibrium under perfect competition:
mcqs.explain: Free entry and exit push price to the minimum point of long-run average cost; at that point P = LMC = LAC (and equals SMC and SAC of the optimum plant), so firms earn only normal profit. "P > LAC" is the trap — any supernormal profit attracts entry until price falls back to minimum LAC. In practice: in highly competitive businesses such as basic garment stitching, margins settle at just covering costs.

mcqs.q: Supernormal profits of competitive firms in the short run will, in the long run, lead to:
options: Entry of new firms and a fall in price
Exit of firms and a rise in price
mcqs.explain: Supernormal profits attract new firms because entry is free; industry supply rises, price falls, and profit is squeezed until only normal profit remains. "Exit of firms and a rise in price" is the trap — that happens when firms are making losses. In practice: when poultry farming in a region becomes very profitable, many new farms come up and broiler prices fall back.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a result of long-run equilibrium under perfect competition?
mcqs.explain: In long-run competitive equilibrium, each firm produces at minimum average cost, with P = MC and only normal profit, so there is no excess capacity. Excess capacity is a feature of monopolistic competition, where firms produce below the minimum-cost output. "Price equal to marginal cost" is the tempting distractor, but it does hold under perfect competition. In practice: this is why perfect competition is the benchmark for efficiency.

mcqs.q: The fundamental cause of monopoly is:
mcqs.explain: Monopoly arises because of barriers to entry — legal (licences, patents), natural (huge economies of scale), or control of key resources — that keep other firms out. "Large number of buyers" is the trap; many buyers exist in most markets and do not create monopoly. In practice: a city gas distribution company with an exclusive authorisation from the PNGRB faces no rival in its area for years.

mcqs.q: A natural monopoly arises when:
options: Economies of scale are so large that one firm can supply the market at lowest cost
mcqs.explain: A natural monopoly exists when economies of scale are so large that one firm can supply the whole market at a lower cost than two or more firms could, so duplicating infrastructure would be wasteful. "A firm owns a patent" is the trap — that is a legal monopoly, not a natural one. In practice: electricity distribution networks and piped water supply are classic natural monopolies, which is why their tariffs are regulated.

mcqs.q: The cross elasticity of demand between a monopolist's product and other goods is:
mcqs.explain: A monopolist sells a product with no close substitutes, so a change in the price of other goods hardly affects its demand — the cross elasticity is zero or very small. "Infinite" is the trap; infinite cross elasticity indicates perfect substitutes, the opposite of monopoly. In practice: competition regulators such as the CCI examine whether close substitutes exist before deciding whether a firm dominates a market.

mcqs.q: For a straight-line demand curve facing a monopolist, the MR curve:
options: Has twice the slope of AR and lies halfway between AR and the price axis
mcqs.explain: If AR is P = a − bQ, then TR = aQ − bQ² and MR = a − 2bQ. So MR has twice the slope of AR and cuts the quantity axis halfway — it lies midway between AR and the price axis. "Coincides with AR" is the trap; that is true only under perfect competition, where price is constant. In practice: pricing analysts use this rule to find the profit-maximising output from a straight-line demand estimate.

mcqs.q: A monopolist faces P = 80 − 2Q and constant MC = ₹20. Its profit-maximising output is:
mcqs.explain: TR = 80Q − 2Q², so MR = 80 − 4Q. Setting MR = MC: 80 − 4Q = 20, so Q = 15 units and price = 80 − 2 × 15 = ₹50. 30 units is the trap — it is the competitive output where P = MC, which a monopolist does not produce. In practice: a monopolist restricts output below the competitive level to keep prices high, which is why regulators watch such firms.

mcqs.q: A monopolist always operates where the price elasticity of demand is:
mcqs.explain: A monopolist sets MR = MC; since MC is positive, MR must also be positive, and MR = P(e − 1)/e is positive only when e is greater than one. So a monopolist always operates on the elastic part of its demand curve. "Less than one" is the trap — there MR would be negative. In practice: if a monopolist found demand inelastic, raising price would increase revenue and cut costs, so it would keep raising price.

mcqs.q: In the long run, a monopolist:
options: Can continue to earn supernormal profit because entry is blocked
mcqs.explain: Because entry is blocked, new firms cannot come in to compete away profits, so a monopolist can keep earning supernormal profit even in the long run. "Always earns only normal profit" is the trap — that is the long-run outcome under perfect and monopolistic competition, where entry is free. In practice: firms holding long-term patents or exclusive licences can sustain high margins for many years.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a condition for price discrimination?
options: Equal price elasticity in all sub-markets
mcqs.explain: Price discrimination needs monopoly power, divisible sub-markets with no resale between them, and different price elasticities in those sub-markets. Equal elasticities are NOT a condition — with equal elasticities, the profit-maximising price would be the same everywhere. "No resale between sub-markets" is the tempting distractor, but it is an essential condition. In practice: railways can charge different fares by class because tickets are not transferable.

mcqs.q: Under price discrimination, a higher price is charged in the market where demand is:
mcqs.explain: A discriminating monopolist charges a higher price where demand is less elastic, because those buyers cut purchases only a little when price rises. "More elastic" is the trap — raising price there would drive many buyers away. In practice: airlines charge last-minute business travellers, whose demand is inelastic, far higher fares than leisure travellers who book weeks ahead.

mcqs.q: At a single price of ₹60, elasticities are 1.5 in market X and 3 in market Y. MR in market Y is:
mcqs.explain: MR = P × (e − 1) ÷ e. In market Y: 60 × (3 − 1) ÷ 3 = 60 × 2 ÷ 3 = ₹40. ₹20 is the trap — it is MR in market X, where elasticity is 1.5: 60 × 0.5 ÷ 1.5. Since MR differs at a single price, shifting sales towards Y raises profit. In practice: this logic is why firms offer lower prices in price-sensitive segments, such as student discounts.

mcqs.q: Charging each buyer the maximum he is willing to pay, so that the whole consumer surplus is taken, is:
mcqs.explain: First-degree (perfect) price discrimination charges each buyer the maximum he is willing to pay, so the seller takes the whole consumer surplus. "Second-degree" is the trap — that varies price with the quantity bought, not with each buyer's maximum. In practice: a doctor or lawyer who negotiates fees according to each client's means comes close to first-degree discrimination.

mcqs.q: Lower per-unit prices for bigger packs, or slab rates for electricity, are examples of:
mcqs.explain: Second-degree price discrimination charges different prices for different quantities or blocks — bigger packs cost less per unit, and electricity tariffs change by slab. "Third-degree" is the trap; that divides buyers into groups, such as students and adults, and charges each group a different price. In practice: Indian state electricity boards use slab tariffs, and FMCG firms offer lower per-gram prices on large packs.

mcqs.q: A discriminating monopolist is in equilibrium when:
options: MRA = MRB = MC of total output
mcqs.explain: A discriminating monopolist first fixes total output where combined MR equals MC, then splits it so that MR in each market equals that same MC: MRA = MRB = MC. If MR differed, moving a unit to the higher-MR market would raise profit. "PA = PB = MC" is the trap — prices differ between markets under discrimination, and a monopolist never sets price equal to MC. In practice: airlines allocate seats across fare classes in this way.

mcqs.q: "X-inefficiency" associated with monopoly refers to:
options: Loss of managerial efficiency where competition is weak or absent
mcqs.explain: X-inefficiency is the loss of managerial efficiency when a firm faces little or no competitive pressure: costs rise above the minimum because managers have no strong reason to control them. "Excess capacity" is the trap — that is a feature of monopolistic competition. In practice: some protected public-sector units historically had bloated costs, which improved once private competition entered their markets.

mcqs.q: In the long run, a firm under monopolistic competition earns:
options: Only normal profit, with excess capacity
mcqs.explain: Under monopolistic competition, free entry wipes out supernormal profit in the long run, so firms earn only normal profit; equilibrium is where the downward-sloping AR is tangent to AC on its falling part, so firms produce below minimum-cost output — excess capacity. "Normal profit at minimum AC" is the trap; that is the perfect-competition outcome. In practice: many restaurants in a city operate with empty tables most of the day.

mcqs.q: The most important form of competition under monopolistic competition is:
options: Non-price competition such as advertising and product differentiation
mcqs.explain: Under monopolistic competition, each firm has a differentiated product, so it competes mainly through non-price methods — advertising, branding, packaging and service — rather than by cutting price. "Price wars" is the trap; these are more typical of oligopoly. In practice: toothpaste and shampoo brands in India spend heavily on advertising and celebrity endorsements to build loyalty.

mcqs.q: The most important feature of oligopoly is:
mcqs.explain: In oligopoly, a few large firms dominate, so each firm's pricing or output decision affects its rivals, and it must anticipate their reactions — interdependence. "Free entry" is the trap — oligopolies usually have significant barriers to entry. In practice: when one Indian cement major raises prices in a region, others typically follow, as each watches the rest closely.

mcqs.q: In the kinked demand curve model, an oligopolist believes rivals will:
options: Follow a price cut but not a price rise
Follow a price rise but not a cut
mcqs.explain: In the kinked demand curve model, an oligopolist expects rivals to match a price cut (to keep their share) but not a price rise (to win its customers). So demand is elastic above the current price and inelastic below it, which keeps prices sticky. "Follow a price rise but not a cut" is the trap — it reverses the assumption. In practice: soft-drink prices in India often stay unchanged for long periods despite cost changes.

mcqs.q: The kinked demand curve hypothesis was given by:
mcqs.explain: The kinked demand curve hypothesis, which explains price rigidity in oligopoly, was put forward by Paul Sweezy in 1939. Cournot is the trap — his duopoly model (1838) has firms choosing output quantities, assuming rivals' output stays fixed. In practice: Sweezy's model is often used to explain why oligopoly prices stay stable even when costs change.

mcqs.q: In which oligopoly model is output the decision variable and firms do not collude?
mcqs.explain: In the Cournot model, firms do not collude and each chooses its output, assuming its rival's output stays fixed. Bertrand is the trap — in Bertrand's model the decision variable is price, not output. In practice: Cournot-type reasoning is used to analyse industries like steel or cement, where firms commit to capacity and output and the market price then adjusts.

mcqs.q: An old, experienced firm that reads market conditions and announces price changes followed by others is a case of:
mcqs.explain: Under barometric price leadership, an old, experienced firm — not necessarily the largest or lowest-cost — reads market conditions well and announces price changes, which others follow as if reading a barometer. "Dominant-firm price leadership" is the trap; there, the leader is the firm with the largest market share. In practice: in some regional markets, one long-established firm is watched by others when deciding seasonal price changes.

mcqs.q: A market with a single buyer and a single seller is:
mcqs.explain: Bilateral monopoly is a market with a single seller (monopoly) facing a single buyer (monopsony); price is settled by bargaining between them. "Monopsony" is the trap — it has a single buyer but can have many sellers. In practice: a sole sugar mill buying cane from a single farmers' co-operative that negotiates for all growers resembles bilateral monopoly, with prices set by negotiation.

mcqs.q: A competitive firm's TC at outputs 30 and 40 units is ₹470 and ₹620 respectively. Its MC per unit over this range is:
mcqs.explain: MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ = (620 − 470) ÷ (40 − 30) = 150 ÷ 10 = ₹15 per unit. ₹15.50 is the trap — it is average total cost at 40 units (620 ÷ 40); ₹150 is the total change in cost, not per unit. In practice: a competitive firm compares this marginal cost with the market price to decide whether producing the extra 10 units adds to profit.

summary: Perfect competition: many firms, homogeneous product, free entry, perfect knowledge; firm is a price taker with P = AR = MR.
Firm equilibrium: MR = MC with MC cutting MR from below; MC above minimum AVC = short-run supply curve.
Short run: supernormal profit (AR > ATC), normal profit (AR = ATC) or loss (AR < ATC, but ≥ AVC).
Long run (PC): entry/exit → normal profit; SMC = LMC = SAC = LAC = P = MR at minimum LAC; optimum firms.
Monopoly: single seller, no close substitute, barriers; AR = demand; MR twice as steep; MR = MC; operates where e > 1; supernormal profit can last.
Price discrimination: needs monopoly power, separable markets, different elasticities, no resale; MRA = MRB = MC; higher price where demand is less elastic. Degrees: first, second, third (Pigou).
Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, free entry, selling costs; long run normal profit with excess capacity.

Oligopoly: few firms, interdependence, selling costs, group behaviour; models — Cournot, Stackelberg, Bertrand, cartel; price leadership (dominant, low-cost, barometric); kinked demand (Sweezy) explains sticky prices.
remember: Normal profit is part of cost (implicit cost).
Monopolist need not produce at minimum LAC; a competitive firm must in the long run.
Duopoly = 2 sellers; monopsony = 1 buyer; oligopsony = few buyers; bilateral monopoly = 1 buyer + 1 seller.
traps: A monopolist is not certain to make profits — demand and cost decide.
Monopolistic competition ≠ monopoly: entry is free.
Under discrimination the higher price goes to the LESS elastic market.
Kinked demand: rivals follow a cut, not a rise — not the other way round.

viva.q: What are the features of perfect competition?
viva.model: Perfect competition has a very large number of buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, and free entry and exit of firms. In addition there is perfect knowledge of market conditions, negligible transaction costs, and every firm is a price taker that must accept the market price.

viva.q: Describe the long-run equilibrium of a firm under perfect competition.
viva.model: In the long run, supernormal profit attracts new firms and losses drive firms out, so price settles where long run average cost is at its lowest. viva.q: Why is marginal revenue less than average revenue for a monopolist?
viva.model: A monopolist faces the downward sloping market demand curve. To sell one more unit it has to lower the price, and the lower price applies to all the units it sells, not just the extra unit. So the addition to total revenue is less than the price. For a straight line demand curve, the MR curve is twice as steep as the AR curve and lies halfway between it and the price axis.

viva.model: First, the seller must have some monopoly power to set prices. Second, the market must be divisible into two or more sub-markets. viva.q: Why is there excess capacity under monopolistic competition in the long run?
viva.model: Under monopolistic competition free entry wipes out supernormal profit, so in the long run the downward sloping demand curve of each firm just touches its average cost curve. Because the demand curve slopes down, this tangency is on the falling part of the average cost curve, to the left of minimum average cost. So each firm produces less than the optimum output and has unused or excess capacity.

viva.q: Explain the kinked demand curve model of oligopoly.
viva.model: The kinked demand curve model was given by Paul Sweezy to explain price rigidity in oligopoly. Each firm believes that rivals will follow a price cut but will not follow a price rise. So the demand curve is elastic above the prevailing price and inelastic below it, giving a kink at the current price. Since neither a rise nor a cut helps, the firm sticks to the prevailing price, which is why prices are sticky.

cases.title: Jaldhara Water Supply — a local monopoly
cases.case: Jaldhara is the only licensed supplier of piped drinking water in a hill town. Its monthly demand (in thousand kilolitres) is P = 400 − 4Q, where P is ₹ per kilolitre. It has a constant average variable cost (= marginal cost) of ₹40 a kilolitre and fixed cost of ₹1,500 thousand a month. The municipality is considering separate tariffs for hotels and households.

mcqs.q: Jaldhara's profit-maximising output (thousand kilolitres) is:
mcqs.explain: TR = 400Q − 4Q², so MR = 400 − 8Q. Setting MR = MC: 400 − 8Q = 40, so Q = 45 thousand kilolitres. 90 is the trap — it is the output where price equals MC (400 − 4Q = 40), the competitive level, not the monopoly level. In practice: this restriction of output is why municipalities regulate tariffs charged by monopoly water suppliers.

mcqs.q: The price it will charge (₹ per kilolitre) is:
mcqs.explain: The monopolist charges the highest price buyers will pay for its chosen output, read from the demand curve: P = 400 − 4 × 45 = 400 − 180 = ₹220 per kilolitre. ₹40 is the trap — it is marginal cost; a monopolist sets price well above MC. ₹180 is the margin over MC. In practice: regulators compare such tariffs with cost to decide whether monopoly suppliers are overcharging.

mcqs.q: Its monthly profit (₹ thousand) is:
mcqs.explain: Profit = (P − AVC) × Q − fixed cost = (220 − 40) × 45 − 1,500 = 8,100 − 1,500 = ₹6,600 thousand. 8,100 is the trap — it is the contribution before deducting the ₹1,500 thousand fixed cost; 9,900 is total revenue. In practice: such sustained supernormal profit is possible only because entry is blocked, which is why utilities often face profit or tariff caps.

mcqs.q: If separate tariffs are allowed and hotels have less elastic demand than households, Jaldhara will:
options: Charge hotels a higher tariff than households
Charge both a tariff equal to MC
mcqs.explain: Under third-degree price discrimination, the higher price goes to the less elastic segment, since those buyers cut use only a little when price rises. Hotels have less elastic demand, so they pay more; piped water cannot be resold, so separate tariffs hold. "Charge households a higher tariff" is the trap — households are the more price-sensitive group. In practice: Indian water and power utilities charge commercial users higher tariffs than households.
